Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

UNITED NATIONS (CNN) -- Bolivian President Evo Morales said Wednesday he does not regret expelling the U.S. ambassador last year, maintaining again that the envoy was plotting with opposition politicians. Bolivian President Evo Morales maintains the U.S. ambassador was plotting against Morales' government. Bolivia declared U.S. Ambassador Philip Goldberg persona non grata in September and ordered him to leave. Goldberg denied that he encouraged anti-government demonstrators to commit violent acts. "I don't regret having expelled the ambassador, Mr. Goldberg," Morales said in an exclusive interview Wednesday with CNN en Español. "And now, with the events we are seeing and we are finding, it is confirmed that he was conspiring against the government, conspiring against the national territory. He is an expert in dividing countries, with external groups and in Bolivia." Morales also expelled a lower-level U.S. diplomat last month, accusing him of contacting opposition groups. Morales indicated Wednesday, however, that he is open to reviewing the issue since President Obama is in office. "With the new times," he said, "we expect to improve diplomatic relations. So we have to revise our politics. You can't conspire against us nor blackmail us. But if there's mutual respect, welcome." Morales also said an assassination plot against him and other government officials that he alleged last week was real. Three gunmen were killed and two others were arrested Thursday after a 30-minute firefight in the city of Santa Cruz. At least two of the gunmen were foreigners, Bolivian authorities said. Morales said last week he had been aware of the assassination plot, which was verified after the arrest of the gunmen. Opposition politicians expressed doubt about the plot, saying Morales had made similar allegations in the past based on flimsy evidence. The gunmen, he said Wednesday, wanted "to take power violently and also undemocratically. But also, if they could not take power, divide a region of the country. ... And for that, they had to take lives." Morales did not mention who might want to divide the country, but five resource-rich eastern regions and the eastern province of Gran Chaco have been seeking greater autonomy. Earlier Wednesday, Morales addressed the United Nations in observance of Earth Day. He called for the nations of the world to accept a set of principles that would protect the planet's resources and "right to life." Morales, the first indigenous president in Bolivia's history, told the U.N. General Assembly that people cannot put their interests above those of the Earth. "Not just human beings have rights, but the planet has rights," he said. "What's happening with climate change is that the rights of Mother Earth are not being respected." Telling the U.N. delegates that "we have the challenge to agree on a universal declaration for the rights of Mother Earth," Morales outlined four principles that he asked them to consider: . Morales pointed out how indigenous people in Bolivia have rites and rituals to honor the Earth. "We now must begin to realize that the Earth does not belong to us," he said. "It's the other way around. We belong to the Earth." Earth Day was started in 1970 in the United States as a way to bring awareness to the ecological problems plaguing the planet. It is celebrated in many parts of the world.

**UNITED NATIONS (CNN) —** Bolivian President Evo Morales said Wednesday that he does not regret expelling the U.S. ambassador last year, reiterating his claim that the envoy had been plotting against his government with opposition politicians.

Bolivia declared U.S. Ambassador Philip Goldberg persona non grata in September and ordered him to leave the country. Goldberg denied encouraging anti-government demonstrators to commit acts of violence.

“I don’t regret having expelled the ambassador, Mr. Goldberg,” Morales said Wednesday in an exclusive interview with CNN en Español. “And now, with the events we are seeing and we are finding, it is confirmed that he was conspiring against the government, conspiring against the national territory. He is an expert in dividing countries, with external groups and in Bolivia.”

Morales also expelled a lower-level U.S. diplomat last month, accusing him of contacting opposition groups. On Wednesday, however, Morales indicated that he was open to reviewing the matter now that President Obama is in office.

“With the new times,” he said, “we expect to improve diplomatic relations. So we have to revise our politics. You can’t conspire against us nor blackmail us. But if there’s mutual respect, welcome.”

Morales also maintained that an alleged assassination plot against him and other government officials, which he disclosed last week, was real.

Three gunmen were killed and two others arrested Thursday following a 30-minute firefight in the city of Santa Cruz. Bolivian authorities said at least two of the gunmen were foreigners.

Morales said last week that he had been aware of the assassination plot and that it was verified following the arrests. Opposition politicians expressed doubts about the plot, saying Morales had made similar allegations in the past based on flimsy evidence.

The gunmen, Morales said Wednesday, wanted “to take power violently and also undemocratically. But also, if they could not take power, divide a region of the country. ... And for that, they had to take lives.”

Morales did not identify who might want to divide the country, but five resource-rich eastern regions and the eastern province of Gran Chaco have been seeking greater autonomy.

Earlier Wednesday, Morales addressed the United Nations in observance of Earth Day. He called on the nations of the world to adopt a set of principles designed to protect the planet’s resources and its “right to life.”

Morales, the first Indigenous president in Bolivia’s history, told the U.N. General Assembly that people cannot place their interests above those of the Earth.

“Not just human beings have rights, but the planet has rights,” he said. “What’s happening with climate change is that the rights of Mother Earth are not being respected.”

Telling U.N. delegates that “we have the challenge to agree on a universal declaration for the rights of Mother Earth,” Morales outlined four principles for their consideration.

Morales noted that Indigenous people in Bolivia observe rites and rituals honoring the Earth.

“We now must begin to realize that the Earth does not belong to us,” he said. “It’s the other way around. We belong to the Earth.”

Earth Day was established in the United States in 1970 to raise awareness of the ecological problems affecting the planet. It is now observed in many parts of the world.

UNITED NATIONS (CNN) — Bolivian President Evo Morales said Wednesday that he stood by his decision to remove the U.S. ambassador the previous year, repeating his claim that the diplomat had worked with opposition leaders against his administration.

In September, Bolivia designated U.S. Ambassador Philip Goldberg persona non grata and instructed him to leave the country. Goldberg rejected accusations that he had urged anti-government protesters to engage in violence.

“I have no regrets about expelling Ambassador Goldberg,” Morales told CNN en Español in an exclusive interview Wednesday. He said recent developments and newly uncovered information confirmed that Goldberg had plotted against both the Bolivian government and the country’s territorial integrity. Morales described the former ambassador as someone experienced in splitting nations through cooperation with foreign and domestic groups.

The Bolivian president also removed a more junior U.S. diplomat last month, alleging that the official had communicated with opposition organizations. However, Morales suggested Wednesday that he was willing to reconsider the broader matter now that Barack Obama was president.

Morales said the changing political climate created an opportunity to strengthen diplomatic ties and reassess Bolivia’s policies. He added that conspiracy and blackmail were unacceptable, but that improved relations would be welcomed if both countries treated each other with respect.

Morales also insisted that a purported plan to assassinate him and other members of his government—an allegation he first raised the previous week—was genuine.

On Thursday, three armed men were killed and two others detained following a 30-minute gun battle in Santa Cruz. Bolivian officials said at least two members of the group were foreign nationals. Morales said he had known about the alleged assassination scheme beforehand and that the arrests confirmed its existence.

Opposition figures questioned the claim, arguing that Morales had previously made similar accusations based on weak evidence.

According to Morales, the armed group intended to seize control by violent, anti-democratic means. If that effort failed, he said, its members planned to separate part of Bolivia from the rest of the country—a goal that would have required killing people.

Morales did not identify those he believed were seeking to break up Bolivia. However, five resource-rich regions in the east, along with the eastern province of Gran Chaco, have pushed for increased autonomy.

Earlier Wednesday, Morales spoke before the United Nations as part of Earth Day observances. He urged countries worldwide to endorse principles designed to safeguard the planet’s natural resources and its “right to life.”

Morales, Bolivia’s first Indigenous president, told the U.N. General Assembly that humanity must not place its own interests ahead of the planet’s needs. He argued that rights belong not only to people but also to Earth, and said climate change demonstrates that the rights of “Mother Earth” are being violated.

He told delegates that the international community faced the task of reaching agreement on a universal declaration recognizing the rights of Mother Earth. Morales then presented four principles for their consideration.

He also noted that Bolivia’s Indigenous communities perform ceremonies and rituals honoring the planet. Humanity must understand, he said, that Earth is not humanity’s possession; rather, people belong to Earth.

Earth Day began in the United States in 1970 as an effort to increase public awareness of environmental problems affecting the planet. The occasion is now observed in many regions around the world.

# Morales defends U.S. envoy’s expulsion, cites alleged assassination plot

**UNITED NATIONS (CNN)** — Bolivian President Evo Morales defended his decision to expel U.S. Ambassador Philip Goldberg, saying an alleged plot to assassinate him showed that foreign-backed groups were working to destabilize his government.

Speaking during an Earth Day appearance at the United Nations, Morales linked the reported conspiracy to political unrest in Bolivia’s eastern lowlands, where opposition leaders had resisted his socialist policies and efforts to increase state control over natural resources.

Bolivian authorities said security forces broke up an armed group during a raid in the eastern city of Santa Cruz. Three suspects were killed and two others arrested. The government alleged that the group had planned attacks against Morales, Vice President Álvaro García Linera and other officials.

Opposition figures questioned the government’s account and called for an independent investigation. U.S. officials denied involvement in any plot against Morales.

Morales expelled Goldberg in September 2008, accusing the ambassador of conspiring with opposition governors. Washington rejected the accusation and responded by expelling Bolivia’s ambassador to the United States.

“I was not wrong,” Morales said in defending the decision, arguing that the alleged assassination plan supported his long-standing claims of outside interference. He did not publicly present evidence directly connecting Goldberg to the reported plot.

The diplomatic dispute unfolded amid deep political divisions in Bolivia. Morales, the country’s first Indigenous president, enjoyed strong support among poor and Indigenous communities, particularly in the western highlands. His opponents were concentrated in wealthier eastern regions, including Santa Cruz, where leaders sought greater regional autonomy.

At the United Nations, Morales also urged governments to recognize environmental protection as a global responsibility and called for greater respect for what Indigenous peoples describe as “Mother Earth.”

His appearance coincided with the U.N. General Assembly’s approval of a Bolivian-sponsored resolution designating April 22 as International Mother Earth Day. Morales said the international community must confront climate change and rethink economic systems that encourage unchecked consumption and exploitation of natural resources.

The resolution was adopted by consensus, reflecting growing international concern over global warming and environmental degradation.

**Morales links Bolivia tensions to alleged plot, urges new U.S. relationship**

**UNITED NATIONS, April 22, 2009** — Bolivian President Evo Morales has renewed accusations of foreign involvement in an alleged plot against his government, even as he appealed for improved relations with Washington and used an Earth Day address at the United Nations to call for sweeping protections for the planet.

In an interview with CNN en Español, Morales said he suspected outside interests had supported a group that Bolivian authorities accuse of planning to assassinate him and encourage the secession of the country’s eastern provinces. He linked the allegations to Bolivia’s long-running tensions with the United States, though publicly available evidence has not established U.S. involvement.

Washington has rejected accusations that it sought to destabilize Morales’s government.

Relations between the two countries have deteriorated sharply since September, when Morales expelled U.S. Ambassador Philip Goldberg, accusing him of conspiring with opposition leaders. The United States denied the charge and expelled Bolivia’s ambassador in response. Morales later ordered the U.S. Drug Enforcement Administration out of Bolivia, alleging that its agents had engaged in political interference.

Morales told CNN he hoped President Barack Obama’s administration would mark a break with past U.S. policy in Latin America. But he said any improvement would require mutual respect and an end to what he described as interference in Bolivia’s domestic affairs.

The latest dispute follows an April 16 police raid at the Hotel Las Américas in Santa Cruz, the center of Bolivia’s conservative opposition. Officers killed three men — Bolivian-Hungarian-Croatian national Eduardo Rózsa-Flores, Irish citizen Michael Dwyer and Árpád Magyarosi, who held Hungarian and Romanian ties — and arrested two others.

The government said the men belonged to an armed cell that had plotted to kill Morales, Vice President Álvaro García Linera and other officials. Authorities also connected the group to earlier bomb attacks and said it sought to promote separatism in the resource-rich eastern lowlands.

Opposition figures and relatives of those killed have challenged the government’s account and called for an independent investigation into whether the men were executed rather than killed in a gunfight. The circumstances of the raid and the full extent of the alleged conspiracy remain disputed.

The case has deepened political divisions between Morales’s leftist government, rooted largely among Indigenous and rural voters in the western highlands, and opposition leaders in Santa Cruz and other eastern departments seeking greater regional autonomy.

At the United Nations on Wednesday, Morales shifted his focus to climate change, telling delegates that the global economic system was placing humanity and nature at risk.

“Capitalism is the worst enemy of humanity,” Morales said, arguing that unlimited industrial growth and consumption were exhausting the Earth’s resources. He urged governments to recognize legal rights for “Mother Earth,” including the rights to life, regeneration, freedom from pollution and ecological balance.

The U.N. General Assembly, acting on a Bolivian-sponsored initiative, proclaimed April 22 as International Mother Earth Day. Morales called the designation a first step toward a broader declaration of planetary rights and said wealthy countries should accept greater responsibility for reducing emissions and helping poorer nations confront climate change.

His appearance combined two central themes of his presidency: resistance to foreign influence and advocacy for Indigenous concepts of humanity’s relationship with nature. But the unresolved Santa Cruz deaths and Bolivia’s confrontation with Washington continued to overshadow his diplomatic message.

### Evo Morales at the United Nations

During an April 2009 visit to United Nations headquarters in New York, Bolivian President Evo Morales promoted a Bolivian-sponsored resolution establishing April 22 as **International Mother Earth Day**. The General Assembly approved the resolution by consensus.

Morales used the visit to discuss Bolivia’s strained relationship with Washington. He defended his September 2008 expulsion of U.S. Ambassador **Philip Goldberg**, accusing Goldberg of meeting with and encouraging opposition leaders seeking greater autonomy for Bolivia’s eastern regions. Morales described him as an expert in separatist conflicts, citing Goldberg’s earlier diplomatic work in the Balkans. The United States denied that Goldberg had conspired against the Bolivian government.

Morales said he was nevertheless hopeful that relations could improve under **President Barack Obama**. He welcomed Obama’s more conciliatory rhetoric but said genuine improvement would require respect for Bolivian sovereignty, an end to political interference, and a relationship based on equality rather than “empire” and subordination.

He also addressed an alleged plot to assassinate him and other senior officials, including Vice President **Álvaro García Linera** and minister **Juan Ramón Quintana**. Bolivian security forces said they had disrupted the plot during an April 16 raid on a hotel in Santa Cruz, killing three alleged members of an armed group and arresting two others. Morales portrayed the group as foreign-linked mercenaries connected to separatist interests. Opposition figures questioned the government’s account and demanded an independent investigation; details surrounding the case remained disputed.

On environmental issues, Morales argued that Indigenous traditions offered an alternative to an economic system that treated nature merely as a commodity. Referring to the Andean concept of **Pachamama**, or Mother Earth, he said human beings belong to the Earth rather than own it. Indigenous principles—communal responsibility, restraint in consumption, and living in harmony with nature—were, in his view, essential to confronting climate change and protecting the planet for future generations.
